cells.tense: You are keeping the practice lit by attention rather than by flash, and the light is holding.
cells.ask: Keep the next session exactly as small as it needs to be, then, right after it, say one true sentence about what it cleared.
cells.core:
You keep the work small and you keep it steady, and you know the difference between what's finished and what you still need. That's why the practice is holding. You're not running on the flash of starting something; the light stays lit because you show up for it without an audience.

It's doing quiet work — you keep going back, and the going back is what keeps the thing alive. The next step is to let out a little more: not to make something new, but to notice what you're freeing up room for. What's carried feels worth carrying because you've kept it that way, not because it kept itself.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the practice lit, and the light is still holding.
cells.verb: turning what's used up into ground for what grows next

cells.tense: You are already arranging the outcome in your head before anything has asked to be arranged.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you're most tempted to finish tonight, close it unfinished, and leave the room for an hour.
cells.core:
You've moved past keeping the practice lit into finishing before it's ready to finish. Some version of this exists ahead of you — everything released, everything renewed — and you're already standing in that room, so your hands are on the light before it needs touching. The end you're rehearsing keeps arriving early, and it keeps costing you the thing you were arranging for.

The way back is to let one thing remain unfinished, and to trust it will still be better in the morning. That may feel like standing in the rain with no umbrella. But the practice doesn't need you to complete it tonight. It needs you to stay with what's actually here.

cells.tense: You stopped picking the practice back up, and the stopping has outlasted the reason it started.
cells.ask: Set a timer for five minutes and do the smallest version of the practice, then say what you noticed out loud to yourself.
cells.core:
You're not keeping anything lit right now. It's not that the skill is gone — you still know how it's done — but you stopped going back, and staying away got easier each time you chose it. You can feel the difference. You know how it feels in your hands when it's steady, and that makes the gap louder, not quieter.

The return is smaller than you think. Start with the smallest version you can stand, and let it get moving on its own before you ask it for anything more. Five minutes tonight and one movement through the practice will do. This isn't a test or a restart back at the beginning. The way back is one small deliberate move, and you're allowed to start there.

cells.tense: You have been clearing and reshaping the space around you without counting it as your own act.
cells.ask: Name one thing you arranged today for someone else's sake, out loud, with no explanation attached.
cells.core:
The room holds its order because you keep it, and people settle in it without knowing why. When something went stale you had already made the space where the next thing could sit. That's the shape of this when it runs clean — quiet upkeep, things working, and nobody having to ask you twice to set something straight.

What's missing is smaller than all that arranging. There's a plainer act underneath: a straight yes or no about what belongs in your space, said without a case built around it. One sentence naming what you did today puts your hand back on the handle where it belongs.
cells.sheetLine: You've been the one arranging this, and nobody has said so.
